## General Definitions & Forms of Polynomials ### Polynomial in One Variable An algebraic expression involving a single variable $x$ with non-negative integral exponents. $$p(x) = a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \dots + a_1 x + a_0$$ Where: * $n$ — degree of the polynomial ($n \ge 0$, integer) * $a_n, a_{n-1}, \dots, a_0$ — real coefficients * $a_n \ne 0$ --- ### Standard Forms by Degree #### Linear Polynomial ($\text{Degree} = 1$) $$p(x) = ax + b$$ > **Condition:** $a \ne 0$ #### Quadratic Polynomial ($\text{Degree} = 2$) $$p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$$ > **Condition:** $a \ne 0$ > #### Cubic Polynomial ($\text{Degree} = 3$) $$p(x) = ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$$ > **Condition:** $a \ne 0$ > --- ## Zeroes of a Polynomial ### Definition of a Zero A real number $k$ is said to be a zero of a polynomial $p(x)$ if: $$p(k) = 0$$ --- ### Zero of a Linear Polynomial For $p(x) = ax + b$ ($a \ne 0$): $$k = -\frac{b}{a} = -\frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x}$$ --- ### Geometrical Representation & Number of Zeroes The zeroes of a polynomial $y = p(x)$ correspond precisely to the $x$-coordinates of the points where the graph intersects the $x$-axis. | Polynomial Type | Degree ($n$) | Graph Shape | Maximum Number of Zeroes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Linear**
| $1$
| Straight line | At most $1$ (exactly $1$ point: $(-\frac{b}{a}, 0)$) | | **Quadratic**
| $2$
| Parabola (opens upward if $a > 0$, downward if $a < 0$) | At most $2$
| | **Cubic**
| $3$
| Continuous curve | At most $3$
| | **Degree $n$**
| $n$
| Continuous curve | At most $n$
| --- ## Relationship Between Zeroes and Coefficients ### Quadratic Polynomial For $p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ ($a \ne 0$) with zeroes $\alpha$ and $\beta$: #### Sum of Zeroes $$\alpha + \beta = -\frac{b}{a} = -\frac{\text{Coefficient of } x}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$$ #### Product of Zeroes $$\alpha \beta = \frac{c}{a} = \frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$$ --- ### Formation of a Quadratic Polynomial A quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is given by: $$p(x) = k \left[ x^2 - (\alpha + \beta)x + \alpha \beta \right]$$ Where: * $k$ — any non-zero real constant ($k \ne 0$) * $(\alpha + \beta)$ — sum of zeroes * $\alpha \beta$ — product of zeroes --- ### Cubic Polynomial (Reference & Extension) For $p(x) = ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$ ($a \ne 0$) with zeroes $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$: #### Sum of Zeroes $$\alpha + \beta + \gamma = -\frac{b}{a} = -\frac{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}{\text{Coefficient of } x^3}$$ #### Sum of Products of Zeroes Taken Two at a Time $$\alpha \beta + \beta \gamma + \gamma \alpha = \frac{c}{a} = \frac{\text{Coefficient of } x}{\text{Coefficient of } x^3}$$ #### Product of Zeroes $$\alpha \beta \gamma = -\frac{d}{a} = -\frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^3}$$ #### Formation of a Cubic Polynomial $$p(x) = k \left[ x^3 - (\alpha + \beta + \gamma)x^2 + (\alpha \beta + \beta \gamma + \gamma \alpha)x - \alpha \beta \gamma \right]$$ Where $k$ is a non-zero real constant. --- ## Algebraic Identities Frequently Used in Polynomial Problems ### Symmetric Functions of Zeroes Useful algebraic forms for calculating values of symmetric expressions of $\alpha$ and $\beta$: $$\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 2\alpha \beta$$ $$(\alpha - \beta)^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4\alpha \beta$$ $$\alpha^3 + \beta^3 = (\alpha + \beta)^3 - 3\alpha \beta(\alpha + \beta)$$ $$\frac{1}{\alpha} + \frac{1}{\beta} = \frac{\alpha + \beta}{\alpha \beta}$$ > **Warning:** Expressions such as $\frac{1}{x-1}$, $\sqrt{x} + 2$, or $x^{-2}$ are **not** polynomials because the exponents of the variable must be non-negative integers. > >
